Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 7 periods = 280 minutes
Total: 7 periods · 4h 40min

periods.activity_title: First Encounter — Reading the Story Aloud

time_bands.activity: The teacher invites students to look at the chapter title and any illustrations on pp.41–44, asking what they notice about the parrot and the merchant. Students share one-word or one-phrase observations aloud.

The teacher reads the full narrative aloud from pp.41–44, pausing briefly at key turns — the merchant refusing freedom, the wild parrot falling from the tree — to allow the scene to register. No questions are posed during this first uninterrupted encounter.
The teacher re-reads pp.44–45 (the escape sequence) aloud, this time inviting students to follow along in their own books and read softly with the teacher. Students track the print with a finger.

The teacher asks two broad oral questions — What surprised you most in the story? and What do you think the wild parrot’s falling-down meant? — and takes four or five quick responses from the class. No written work is required.

periods.teacher_notes: This is the class’s first encounter with the narrative, so the goal is absorption and curiosity rather than comprehension drilling. The story’s turning point — the coded message sent by the wild parrot — is easy to miss on a first reading; a brief pause at that moment helps students hold it before deeper work begins.

periods.activity_title: Comprehension Discussion — Questions on the Narrative

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Think A (p.45): answer five comprehension questions on the narrative.

time_bands.activity: The teacher conducts a brief shared re-reading of the merchant’s journey passage (pp.43–44) to refresh the plot details students will need for the questions. One or two volunteers read sentences aloud.

Let us Think A — “five comprehension questions on the story” (p.45): the teacher poses questions 1, 2, and 3 orally one at a time, giving students a moment to think-pair-share before the class agrees on a response. The teacher writes key phrases from accepted answers on the board.

Let us Think A — questions 4 and 5 are addressed. For question 5 (how the parrot escaped), the teacher guides students to reconstruct the full sequence — coded message, playing dead, windowsill, flight — building a brief chain-of-events on the board using student responses.
Students write answers to any two questions of their choice from Let us Think A in their notebooks, using the board’s key phrases as a scaffold. The teacher circulates and offers brief feedback.

periods.teacher_notes: Having heard the story read aloud together, students are now ready to unpack it through sustained discussion. The escape sequence (question 5) is the conceptually richest question — it requires students to treat the wild parrot’s falling-down as a deliberate act of communication, which is the story’s central insight.

periods.activity_title: Discussion, Listening and Speaking — Voices on Freedom

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Think B (p.45): discuss three reflective questions on freedom and intelligence.
Let us Listen (p.48): listen to paragraph on bird sanctuaries; respond to teacher’s oral questions.

time_bands.activity: Let us Think B — “three discussion prompts on freedom and wisdom” (p.45): the teacher poses each prompt in turn. For each, students think briefly in pairs, then one or two pairs share with the class. The teacher models expanding a short answer into a full sentence.
Let us Listen — “listening paragraph on bird sanctuaries” (p.48): the teacher reads the paragraph aloud clearly at a natural pace, repeating it three times. Students listen without writing.

Following the listening paragraph, the teacher asks factual oral questions — What are bird sanctuaries built for? Which is the oldest in India? Where is the Bharatpur sanctuary? Students respond orally; the teacher confirms or gently corrects each answer.

The teacher invites students to connect the listening passage to the story — asking whether the parrot in the story needed a sanctuary or something else entirely. Three or four brief responses close the unit.

periods.teacher_notes: The three Let us Think B prompts are genuinely open — there is no single correct answer — so the teacher’s role is to prompt elaboration rather than validate one view. The listening paragraph introduces factual content about bird sanctuaries; students who recall the merchant’s forest journey may notice the contrast between wild habitats and protected reserves.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Speak A (p.48): listen and repeat word pairs distinguishing ‘ai’ and ‘oi’ sounds.
Let us Speak B (p.49): look at caged and free parrot pictures; share views on which bird you’d be and why.

time_bands.activity: Let us Speak A — “word-pair repetition drill distinguishing ‘ai’ and ‘oi’ sounds” (p.48): the teacher says each pair (tail/toil, bail/boil, ail/oil, fail/foil, cane/coin, sail/soil) clearly, students repeat chorally. The pairs are then repeated with individual students, the teacher listening for accurate vowel distinction.

The teacher writes the six pairs on the board and underlines the vowel cluster in each word. Students identify the pattern and the teacher confirms that ‘ai’ and ‘oi’ feel different in the mouth — demonstrating the lip position briefly.

Let us Speak B — “caged and free parrot picture-based oral sharing” (p.49): the teacher asks students to look at the two pictures in their textbook. Each student takes a moment to decide their choice, then four to six students share their view in one or two sentences with the class.

The teacher facilitates a quick class poll — hands up for the free parrot, hands up for the caged parrot — and invites one representative from each side to give a final sentence. The teacher affirms the diversity of views without adjudicating.

periods.teacher_notes: The ‘ai’ / ‘oi’ distinction is a genuine phonemic contrast that students at this stage often flatten; choral repetition followed by individual attempts is the most reliable way to make the difference audible. The picture-based speaking task draws on the story’s central tension, so students who engaged with Let us Think B will have richer things to say.

periods.activity_title: Phrasal Verbs, Collective Nouns and Present Perfect

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Learn A (p.46): fill blanks in a paragraph using seven phrasal-verb phrases from a word bank.
Let us Learn B (p.46): complete sentences with correct collective nouns from a word bank.

homework.task_brief: Let us Learn C (pp.47–48): complete five sentences using present perfect tense forms.

time_bands.activity: The teacher writes three of the phrasal verbs on the board (came across, stepped out, look after) and asks students to guess each meaning from context, pointing to familiar situations — ‘came across a puppy’, ‘stepped out of home’. Students suggest meanings aloud.

Let us Learn A — “fill-in-the-blanks paragraph using phrasal-verb word bank” (p.46): the teacher reads the incomplete paragraph aloud once. Students work individually to fill all seven blanks, then the class reviews each answer together, the teacher confirming and briefly explaining any wrong choices.

Let us Learn B — “collective noun fill-in sentences” (p.46): the teacher writes the word bank on the board (pack, bouquet, army, flock, bunch, flight, swarm) and points out that the chapter itself uses ‘a flock of parrots’. Students complete the six sentences; the class reviews answers together.

The teacher reads Let us Learn C (pp.47–48) aloud, presenting the present perfect rule and the two model sentences. Students copy the rule and the two examples into their notebooks. The teacher sets the sentence-completion exercise as homework and explains what ‘has/have + past participle’ means with one additional quick example.

periods.teacher_notes: Phrasal verbs and collective nouns are both vocabulary concepts that emerge directly from the story — the merchant ‘came across’ the flock, and a ‘flight of parrots’ is the very group he meets. Anchoring these terms to story moments helps students remember them. Present perfect is introduced here and practised as homework because the grammar concept needs consolidation beyond a single in-class pass.

periods.activity_title: Imaginative Writing — The Parrot’s Life After Freedom

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Write (p.49): plan and draft a short imaginative continuation of the parrot’s story after its escape.

time_bands.activity: The teacher revisits the story’s final image — the parrot spreading its wings and flying from the windowsill — by reading those two sentences aloud from p.45. The teacher then writes three open questions on the board: Where did the parrot fly? Who did it meet? What did it do next? Students think silently for a moment.

Modelled writing: the teacher thinks aloud and writes a model opening sentence on the board — ‘After escaping from the golden cage, the parrot decided to fly away to the tall mango tree at the edge of the forest.’ The teacher names the choices made — a place, a direction, a vivid detail — and invites students to suggest one change to the model sentence.

Let us Write — “imaginative story continuation beginning ‘After escaping…’” (p.49): students write their own three-to-five sentence continuation in their notebooks using the board questions as a guide. The teacher circulates, offering one-sentence encouragement or a brief nudge on word choice.

Three or four volunteers read their continuations aloud. After each reading, the teacher asks the class one appreciative question — What detail did you like? — to build a listening culture. The teacher notes two or three strong phrases on the board from student work.

Students re-read their own draft quietly and make one small revision — adding a detail, changing a word — before closing their notebooks. No collection is required; the goal is a completed draft in the student’s own hand.

periods.teacher_notes: The writing prompt asks students to extend a narrative whose ending is already satisfying — the challenge is imagining what freedom actually looks like for the parrot. The modelled sentence on the board is meant to be replaced, not copied; students who try to copy it wholesale should be gently redirected to the story’s own imagery for their own ideas.

periods.activity_title: Bird Feeders and Bird Facts — Hands-On Extension

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us Do (pp.50–51): identify materials used in six bird-feeder pictures and plan a feeder to make at home.
Let us Explore (p.52): choose two birds from the illustrated list and share interesting facts with the class.

time_bands.activity: Let us Do — “identify materials in six bird-feeder pictures” (pp.50–51): students open their textbooks and look at the six feeder pictures. The teacher points to each in turn and asks the class to name the material aloud — plastic bottle, coconut shell, bamboo log, ice-cream stick box, clay bowl, juice carton. Students respond chorally and then individually.

The teacher asks students to choose one feeder type they could realistically make at home and to describe in one sentence what they would fill it with and where they would place it. Six to eight students share their plan aloud. The teacher writes a brief planning template on the board: Material — Contents — Location.

Let us Explore — “choose two birds from the illustrated list and share facts” (p.52): students look at the ten labelled bird pictures and choose two. They spend three minutes looking at the pictures and thinking of one or two facts they already know about each choice. Students then share with a partner before four pairs share with the class.

The teacher closes by connecting the bird-feeder and bird-facts activities to the story’s theme — the parrot wanted to live in the wild, and these activities help students think about what wild birds actually need. Students are invited to make their feeder at home with a parent’s help, as the textbook suggests.

periods.teacher_notes: The bird-feeder identification is an observational task that works with the textbook pictures alone — no physical materials need to be in the classroom. For Let us Explore, students are drawing on what they already know about familiar birds like sparrows and crows; the teacher should validate everyday knowledge as a legitimate starting point for curiosity.

items.item_stem: When the merchant returned home and told the caged parrot about the wild parrot falling from the tree, the caged parrot also fell to the cage floor. Why did the caged parrot do this?

options.label: A
options.text: It understood the wild parrot’s coded message and pretended to be dead so the merchant would remove it from the cage.

options.label: B
options.text: It wanted the merchant to feel sorry and bring it a gift.

options.label: C
options.text: It was frightened by the merchant’s loud voice.

options.label: D
options.text: It was genuinely ill and collapsed from weakness.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Student may have missed that the parrot acted deliberately rather than out of fear.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student may have taken the parrot’s collapse literally rather than as a ruse.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Student has confused the parrot’s earlier request for gifts with the escape strategy.

items.source_lo: Student retrieves information and infers character motivation using a narrative as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Merchant, caged parrot, coded message, wild parrot falling, escape through feigned death.
items.item_stem: The story shows that the caged parrot chose to send a secret message rather than simply ask for freedom again. What does this choice tell us about the parrot’s character? Write two to three sentences using details from the story.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: The parrot’s choice shows it was clever and patient. Instead of repeating a request the merchant had already refused, it worked out a plan using the wild parrot’s coded behaviour, proving that it could think beyond its situation to find a solution.

items.item_stem: Your teacher will read a short paragraph about bird sanctuaries aloud. Listen carefully. Then answer: Which bird sanctuary in the passage is described as the oldest in India, and in which state is it located?

options.text: The Bharatpur Bird Sanctuary is the largest bird sanctuary in India.
The Vedanthangal Bird Sanctuary is located in Rajasthan.
The Vedanthangal Bird Sanctuary is the oldest bird sanctuary in India.
There are more than 100 bird sanctuaries in India.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Statement 1 — True. The Vedanthangal Bird Sanctuary, located in Tamil Nadu, is the oldest bird sanctuary in India. Statement 2 — False; Vedanthangal is in Tamil Nadu, not Rajasthan. Statement 3 — True. The Bharatpur Bird Sanctuary in Rajasthan is the largest. Statement 4 — False; the passage states there are more than 70 bird sanctuaries, not 100.

items.item_stem: After the parrot flew away from the merchant’s window, it finally found itself free. Write one sentence describing the very first thing the parrot did after it flew out of sight of the merchant’s house.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Accept any sentence that names a concrete first action (e.g. landing on a tree, calling out to other birds, flying towards the jungle) and is written as a complete sentence. The action must be something a free bird could plausibly do.
